resources.string: Shells on machines you added by hand.
Add a machine you can reach over SSH, and open a shell on it from here.
%1$s will ask for a password the next time you open a shell. Nothing on the server itself is touched, and any key already in authorized_keys stays there.
Name is what the row is called; leave it empty and the host is used. The port is 22 unless your server says otherwise.
Enter the host name or address.
That is not a host name. Leave out the user name and any ssh:// prefix.
The port has to be a number from 1 to 65535.
Enter the user to sign in as.
A tap on this server opens a shell straight away.
Six digits, kept in this phone\'s secure storage. Setting the lock back to Nothing forgets it.
Your fingerprint, face or screen lock is asked for before the shell opens.
Once more, to be sure of it.
Those two did not match. Start again.
You will be asked for this before this server opens.
You are asked for the password when you open a shell. Choose Remember it in that prompt to keep it in this phone\'s secure storage.

A key replaces the password for this server, it does not sit beside one. The private half is kept in this phone\'s secure storage; the public half is the line you put in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the server.
Switching to a password forgets the saved key when you save. Nothing on the server changes.
Append this line to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the server. The private half stays in this phone\'s secure storage and is never sent anywhere except as a signature.
For a server you have not set up a key for yet. It is an ed25519 key, the kind OpenSSH makes by default.
.ssh/id_ed25519 on the machine you made the key on. Move it across with a cable or a cloud drive.
The private half, not the public one. If what you have starts with ssh-ed25519, that is the half the server wants.
Only a label. It is what the server shows beside the key, and it tells your key apart from the one your laptop uses.
Only if the key has one. It is kept in this phone\'s secure storage beside the key, because a phone has no ssh-agent to ask.

That is not a private key. A private key starts with -----BEGIN OPENSSH PRIVATE KEY-----. If you pasted a line starting with ssh-ed25519, that is the public half, which goes on the server rather than here.
This key could not be read: %1$s
This key has a passphrase. Type it so the app can unlock the key when it connects.
That passphrase did not unlock this key.
That file could not be read.
This is the first time you have connected to %1$s. Check its fingerprint against the server itself. Most providers show it in their console, and ssh-keygen -lf prints it on the box.
The server\'s key has changed since you last connected. If this was not you, do not continue.
If you reinstalled the server, or know why its key changed, use Forget its key in the server\'s menu and connect again. If you do not, someone may be sitting between you and the server.
You did not accept this server\'s key.
The server did not accept this key. Check that its public half is in authorized_keys.
The server did not answer in time.
The shells on the server stop, along with anything running in them.
This connection has ended. Open the server again to browse its files.
A list of tunnels to set up. Each one listens on this phone only, so another app on the phone can reach a service the server can see.
A forward runs for as long as this connection does. Closing it, or leaving the app for long enough, ends it, and nothing here keeps it alive in the background.
The port another app on this phone will connect to. localhost:%1$s is what you point it at.
Where the server connects to, seen from the server. This can be 127.0.0.1 for a service that only listens on the server itself, or a name that resolves only from the server.
A forward runs for as long as the connection to this server does. There is no way to keep one running in the background.
The local port has to be a number.
The local port has to be between 1 and 65535.
The port on the server has to be a number.
The port on the server has to be between 1 and 65535.
Say which machine the server should connect to. It is the machine at the far end of the tunnel, and it is the server that does the connecting.
That is not a host name or an address. Letters, digits, dots, colons, underscores and hyphens only.
This server already forwards %1$d. Two forwards cannot listen on the same port, so one of them would never start.
